topics.name: Poseidon
topics.kicker: Greek god of the sea, earthquakes, and horses · Brother of Zeus
topics.dates: Worshipped across ancient Greece for over 1,000 years
topics.briefing: Poseidon ruled the restless, storm-tossed sea the way his brother Zeus ruled the sky. He carried a three-pronged trident that could shatter the earth itself, raced across the waves in a chariot pulled by horse-fish monsters, and was sore loser enough to flood a city after losing a contest to Athena. Sailors prayed to him before every voyage, just in case.

tossups.p: As an infant, this god was swallowed by his father, Cronus, and later freed when Zeus forced Cronus to vomit up his children. This deity sided with the Greeks in the Trojan War because of a grudge against King Laomedon, who refused to pay him.
tossups.r: This god is sometimes called the secret father of the hero Theseus. For 10 points, name this trident-wielding brother of Zeus and Hades, the Greek god of the sea.

tossups.p: This god sent his son Halirrhothius [“hal-ih-ROH-thee-us”] to chop down one of Athena’s sacred olive trees after losing a contest to her. He is sometimes honored with the Isthmian Games, one of the four great Panhellenic athletic festivals held in ancient Greece. Furious at King Laomedon for refusing to pay him, this god sent a sea monster to menace the city of Troy until the hero Heracles killed it.
tossups.r: Homer calls him “Earth-Shaker” for causing quakes by striking the ground. For 10 points, name this Greek god of the sea, brother of Zeus and Hades.

tossups.p: This god fathered the winged horse Pegasus with the Gorgon Medusa, and fathered the talking horse Arion after chasing Demeter, who had turned herself into a mare to escape him. He cursed Minos’s wife, Pasiphaë [“pah-SIF-ah-ee”], to fall in love with a bull after Minos refused to sacrifice it to him, a curse that produced the Minotaur.
tossups.r: Many other monstrous or heroic sons are credited to this god, including the giant Antaeus and the one-eyed Cyclops Polyphemus. For 10 points, name this horse-loving Greek god of the sea.

tossups.p: Along with Apollo, this god was hired by King Laomedon to build the walls of Troy, then stiffed on the payment. This deity rides a chariot pulled by hippocamps, half-horse and half-fish creatures, and is the husband of the sea-nymph Amphitrite [“am-fih-TRY-tee”]. After the Trojan War ended, this god tore down the Greek wall around their beached ships by unleashing every river on it at once.
tossups.r: He is said to have created the very first horse. For 10 points, name this trident-carrying brother of Zeus, the Greek god of the sea and earthquakes.

trap.title: Is “Neptune” ever okay?
trap.body: Poseidon is the Greek sea god; Neptune is his Roman counterpart, a separate answer line with his own (very similar) myths. Most modern tournaments explicitly say “do not accept or prompt on Neptune,” though a few older sets do allow it. There is also a shared lead-in trap: early clues about building Troy’s walls for Laomedon fit both Poseidon and his nephew Apollo equally well, since they did the job together.
trap.fix: Never volunteer “Neptune” unless you hear the judge announce it is accepted for that specific question. On a Troy-walls clue, wait for a detail that splits the two gods apart — a sea monster means Poseidon, a plague means Apollo.
trap.line: Real answer line: Poseidon (most sets: “do not accept or prompt on Neptune”).

topics.name: Artemis
topics.kicker: Greek goddess of the hunt and the moon · Twin sister of Apollo
topics.dates: Honored across ancient Greece for well over 1,000 years
topics.briefing: Artemis grew up fast: legend says she helped deliver her own twin brother, Apollo, just moments after she herself was born on the island of Delos. As goddess of the hunt and the moon, she roamed the wilderness with a silver bow and a pack of hounds, and she had a fierce, no-exceptions rule — anyone who disrespected her paid for it, like the hunter Actaeon, whom she turned into a stag for spying on her.

trap.title: Diana, but watch the timing
trap.body: Artemis is the Greek goddess; Diana is her Roman counterpart. Unlike Neptune for Poseidon, many tournaments DO accept “Diana” — though some only until the question says the word “Greek,” after which only “Artemis” counts. She is also one of three eternally virgin Olympians, along with Athena and Hestia, so a clue about refusing marriage alone isn’t enough to buzz.
trap.fix: “Diana” is usually safe early on, but once you hear “Greek goddess,” switch your answer to “Artemis.” And wait for a clue specific to the hunt, the moon, or her twin brother Apollo before buzzing on the virgin-goddess theme alone — it could be Athena or Hestia instead.

topics.name: Apollo
topics.kicker: Greek god of the sun, music, and prophecy · Twin brother of Artemis
topics.dates: Delphi oracle active for over 1,000 years
topics.briefing: Apollo could heal with a touch and cause a plague with an arrow, which made him one of the most feared and respected gods on Mount Olympus. Twin brother of Artemis and god of the sun, music, and prophecy, he killed the monstrous serpent Python at Delphi and set up the famous Oracle there, where a priestess answered questions from kings and ordinary people alike for over a thousand years.

tossups.r: He once used that power to punish the Greek army after Agamemnon angered this god’s priest, Chryses, by refusing to free his captured daughter. For 10 points, name this Greek god of prophecy, archery, and the sun.

tossups.r: This god pursued the nymph Daphne, who escaped by transforming into a laurel tree. For 10 points, name this twin brother of Artemis, the Greek god of music, prophecy, and the sun.

trap.title: Sun god… or is he?
trap.body: Later Greek and Roman poetry often calls Apollo the sun god, but in the oldest myths, the actual Titan of the sun is Helios, a separate figure who drives a sun chariot across the sky. The two gods get blended together in many retellings, so a clue just about “the sun” could mean either one unless it also mentions music, prophecy, archery, or his twin sister Artemis. He also shares an early lead-in with his uncle Poseidon: both gods built the walls of Troy for King Laomedon.
trap.fix: Don’t buzz on “sun god” alone — wait for a second clue (music, prophecy, Delphi, the lyre, or Artemis) that points specifically to Apollo rather than Helios. On a Troy-walls clue, listen for whether the question says “plague” (Apollo) or “sea monster” (Poseidon) before you answer.

tossups.p: This hero’s fatal duel with his own son has a famous parallel in the Persian warrior Rostam’s tragic fight with his son Sohrab. Tricked into breaking his sacred vow never to eat dog meat, this man kept fighting even after his charioteer, Laeg, was killed by one of Lugaid’s spears.

tossups.p: Some myths name this man’s father as the god Lugh, with the warrior Sualtam raising him as a foster son. As a boy eavesdropping on the druid Cathbad’s prophecy, he learned that taking up arms that day would bring a short life but eternal glory — and begged his uncle for weapons anyway.
tossups.r: After training under the warrior-woman Scáthach on an island off Scotland, he later killed his own son, Connla, after the boy refused to break a vow by revealing his name. For 10 points, name this Irish hero who wielded the barbed spear Gáe Bulg.

tossups.p: The war goddess the Morrígan attacked this man as an eel, a wolf, and a hornless heifer after he spurned her advances, and he wounded her each time. After his death, she landed on his shoulder as a raven to show his enemies he had finally fallen.
tossups.r: In combat, his body would twist into a monstrous shape called the “warp spasm,” with one eye bulging out and the other sinking in. For 10 points, name this hero who, as a boy, killed a smith’s guard dog and took its place until a replacement could be raised.

tossups.p: At Bricriu’s Feast, this man was the only guest willing to let a disguised Cú Roí behead him in return, after beheading Cú Roí first, and so won the champion’s portion. His myths were retold in English by Lady Gregory in the early 1900s.
tossups.r: He courted his wife, Emer, through a difficult series of riddles before winning her hand. For 10 points, name this nephew of King Conchobar, a hero of Ulster who wielded the spear Gáe Bulg.

trap.title: Which “Cú”? (And whose son?)
trap.body: A rival hero named Cú Roí shares the “Cú” (hound) part of this man’s name and even appears in his myths as an opponent. tossups.p: A medieval text called the _Book of Invasions_ describes a series of mythical peoples who settled this island and their battles with the monstrous Fomorians, led by the one-eyed giant Balor. Another group in that text, the Tuatha Dé Danann, were a race of magical beings named for the goddess Danu.
tossups.r: Those gods were eventually driven to live underground by invaders called the Milesians. For 10 points, name this island whose folklore also includes leprechauns and pots of gold.

tossups.p: The god Lugh killed his own tyrannical grandfather, Balor, with a sling stone through his one giant eye at a battle fought on this island’s plain of Mag Tuired. In another tale, four children of the god Lir were turned into swans by a jealous stepmother for 900 years.
tossups.r: This island’s hero Cú Chulainn single-handedly defended Ulster against Queen Medb’s cattle raid. For 10 points, name this country, legendarily home to a chief god called the Dagda and his bottomless cauldron.

tossups.p: According to legend, the poet Oisín returned from the magical land of Tír na nÓg to this island after what felt like three years, only to instantly turn into an old man when he touched the ground. Oisín’s father, Fionn mac Cumhaill, gained all the world’s wisdom from one taste of the Salmon of Knowledge.
tossups.r: A trio of sisters making up the crow goddess the Morrígan could spread fear and panic on this island’s battlefields. For 10 points, Saint Patrick legendarily drove all the snakes out of what island country?

tossups.p: In one tale, the giant Fionn mac Cumhaill’s quick-thinking wife disguised him as a baby to trick a rival Scottish giant, Benandonner, into fleeing in fright. That same Fionn is said to have built the Giant’s Causeway, connecting this island to Scotland.
tossups.r: This island’s Queen Medb led a famous raid to steal a prized bull in the _Táin Bó Cúailnge_, the Cattle Raid of Cooley. For 10 points, name this country, home to Dublin and the legendary hero Cú Chulainn.

tossups.p: The Milesians, Gaelic-speaking invaders said to have come from Spain, conquered this island’s earlier divine inhabitants, the Tuatha Dé Danann, who then withdrew to live in hidden mounds called the sídhe. The ancient festival of Samhain, later a root of Halloween, marked the start of winter on this island.
tossups.r: This island’s hero Fionn mac Cumhaill led a band of warriors called the Fianna. For 10 points, name this “Emerald Isle,” legendary home of leprechauns and banshees.

tossups.p: This island’s folklore includes wailing female spirits called banshees, who are said to warn families of a coming death. In its most famous epic, a single hero wielding a barbed spear called the Gáe Bulg held off an entire army alone to protect the province of Ulster.
tossups.r: That hero, Cú Chulainn, fought for this island’s province of Ulster against the forces of Queen Medb. For 10 points, name this country whose mythical former rulers included the magical Tuatha Dé Danann.

tossups.p: A bottomless cauldron of plenty belonged to the Dagda, a chief god of this island’s mythical Tuatha Dé Danann. According to the _Book of Invasions_, those gods took control of this island by defeating an earlier people called the Fir Bolg.
tossups.r: Fionn mac Cumhaill accidentally gained all wisdom by tasting the Salmon of Knowledge while cooking it for his teacher on this island. For 10 points, name this country, legendary home of the hero Cú Chulainn.

tossups.p: Niamh, a princess from the Land of Youth, fell in love with the poet Oisín and brought him away from this island for what he thought was only a few years. This island’s one-eyed giant Balor led the monstrous Fomorians against the Tuatha Dé Danann at the Battle of Mag Tuired.
tossups.r: This island’s Giant’s Causeway was supposedly built by the giant Fionn mac Cumhaill. For 10 points, name this island nation, home to Dublin and Saint Patrick.

tossups.p: Three sisters, Badb, Macha, and Nemain, together made up this island’s crow-shaped war goddess, the Morrígan. This island’s divine Tuatha Dé Danann were eventually defeated by Gaelic-speaking invaders called the Milesians and withdrew to live in the sídhe mounds.
tossups.r: In this island’s best-known epic, Queen Medb led a raid to steal a bull in the Cattle Raid of Cooley. For 10 points, what island country’s folklore also features leprechauns who guard pots of gold?

tossups.p: This island’s hero Fionn mac Cumhaill is said to have built a rock causeway to Scotland to fight a rival giant he later tricked by disguising himself as a baby. This island’s war goddess the Morrígan could shapeshift into an eel, a wolf, or a heifer.
tossups.r: That goddess is sometimes grouped as three sisters who spread panic in battle on this island. For 10 points, name this country, legendary setting of the Ulster Cycle and the Cattle Raid of Cooley.

tossups.p: According to the _Book of Invasions_, a race of gods called the Tuatha Dé Danann ruled this island until Gaelic-speaking Milesians arrived from Spain and drove them underground. This island’s chief god, the Dagda, owned a cauldron that never ran empty and a club that could kill with one end and heal with the other.
tossups.r: This island’s hero Cú Chulainn earned his name after killing a smith’s guard dog as a boy. For 10 points, name this country, legendary home of banshees and leprechauns.

tossups.r: This island’s hero Fionn mac Cumhaill tasted the Salmon of Knowledge and gained all the world’s wisdom. For 10 points, Saint Patrick is said to have driven every snake out of this country.

trap.title: Perseus, or Percy Jackson?
trap.body: Rick Riordan’s modern book and movie hero Percy Jackson is short for “Perseus Jackson,” and a real quiz bowl answer line exists for him too. Percy fights monsters, carries a magic weapon, and goes on quests just like the original Perseus — but Percy is the son of Poseidon, not Zeus, attends Camp Half-Blood, and wields a sword named Anaklusmos, or Riptide.
trap.fix: Zeus, Danaë, Medusa, Andromeda, and Mycenae point to the ancient Greek hero. Poseidon, Camp Half-Blood, Grover, and Riptide point to Percy Jackson, a completely different answer.
trap.line: Real answer line: Perseus. A separate real answer line, Percy Jackson [accept either underlined portion; accept Perseus Jackson], is a different character.

topics.name: Jason
topics.kicker: Leader of the Argonauts · Sailed the Argo for the Golden Fleece
topics.briefing: Jason was a Greek hero whose scheming uncle Pelias sent him on what looked like an impossible quest: sail to the edge of the known world and steal the Golden Fleece. He recruited the greatest heroes in Greece, including Heracles and the musician Orpheus, to crew his ship, the _Argo_. He only pulled it off with help from the clever sorceress Medea, whom he later betrayed, with tragic results for them both.

tossups.p: As an infant, this man was secretly raised by the centaur Chiron after his uncle seized his father’s throne in Iolcus. Years later, the craftsman Argus built this man a fifty-oared ship with help from the goddess Athena, who fitted its prow with a piece of prophetic oak from Zeus’s grove at Dodona.
tossups.r: Orpheus once drowned out the deadly song of the Sirens with his lyre to protect this man’s crew. For 10 points, name this captain of the Argo who led the Argonauts on the quest for the Golden Fleece.

tossups.p: This man arrived in Iolcus wearing only one sandal, having lost the other crossing a river, which alarmed his uncle when an old prophecy was recalled. On the island of Lemnos, this man and his crew were welcomed by Queen Hypsipyle and her husbandless subjects.
tossups.r: This man’s crew later drove off the Harpies tormenting the blind prophet Phineus, who repaid them with directions to Colchis. For 10 points, name this leader of the Argonauts, who sought the Golden Fleece.

tossups.p: This man’s ship passed safely through the crashing Symplegades [“sim-pleh-GAH-deez”], or Clashing Rocks, after its crew sent a dove through the gap first. At Colchis, King Aeetes told this man that he could only have the Golden Fleece if he could yoke a pair of fire-breathing bronze bulls and plow a field with them.
tossups.r: He then sowed a dragon’s teeth into that same field and watched armed warriors spring up from the furrows. For 10 points, name this hero who led the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece.

tossups.p: This man defeated the warriors who sprouted from a dragon’s teeth he had sown by tossing a rock into their ranks, tricking them into killing each other. The Fleece itself hung in a sacred grove guarded by a dragon that never slept, until this man’s companion sang it into slumber.
tossups.r: That companion was the sorceress Medea, who helped this man steal the Fleece and later became his wife. For 10 points, name this captain of the Argo and leader of the Argonauts.

tossups.p: Fleeing Colchis with the stolen Fleece, this man’s new wife killed her own brother, Apsyrtus, to slow down their pursuers. Earlier on the voyage, this man’s crewmate Heracles had been left behind while searching for his companion Hylas, who was pulled into a spring by water nymphs.
tossups.r: This man’s ship, built by Argus with Athena’s help, carried a speaking plank cut from an oak at Dodona. For 10 points, name this Greek hero who led the Argonauts on the quest for the Golden Fleece.

tossups.p: Back in Iolcus, this man’s wife tricked the daughters of his wicked uncle Pelias into trying a deadly spell on their own father, falsely promising that the magic that made an old ram young again would work on him too. That trick killed Pelias instead.
tossups.r: This man and his wife, Medea, were then exiled to Corinth. For 10 points, name this hero who had led the Argonauts in the quest for the Golden Fleece before his uncle’s death.

tossups.p: Years after returning from Colchis, this man abandoned his sorceress wife to marry Glauce, a princess of Corinth also called Creusa. His jilted wife sent the new bride a cursed golden robe and crown as a wedding gift, which burned her to death.
tossups.r: That same wife, Medea, then killed the two sons she had with this man, as revenge for his betrayal, before escaping in a chariot lent by her grandfather, the sun god Helios. For 10 points, name this hero and former leader of the Argonauts.

tossups.p: This man’s uncle had seized the throne of Iolcus from this man’s father and then sent this man on a near-impossible quest, hoping he would never return. On the way to complete it, this man’s crew rescued the blind seer Phineus from a flock of Harpies that kept stealing his food.
tossups.r: Phineus then told this man how to sail the Argo through the Clashing Rocks. For 10 points, name this nephew of King Pelias who led the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece.

tossups.p: This man’s crew included the only woman among the Argonauts, the huntress Atalanta, as well as the twins Castor and Pollux. This man completed deadly trials set by King Aeetes of Colchis, including yoking bulls that breathed fire, with help from the king’s daughter.
tossups.r: That princess, the sorceress Medea, helped him defeat an army sprung from dragon’s teeth. For 10 points, name this captain of the Argo who sought the Golden Fleece to reclaim his throne from Pelias.

tossups.p: According to one legend, this man founded the city of Ljubljana after slaying a dragon there on his way home from his most famous voyage. In another tale, this man’s half-rotten ship later collapsed and killed him while he rested in its shade.
tossups.r: Earlier, Orpheus’s music had saved this man’s crew from the Sirens. For 10 points, name this Greek hero who commanded the Argo and its crew of Argonauts on the quest for the Golden Fleece.

tossups.p: This man’s father-in-law, King Aeetes of Colchis, demanded that he plow a field with bronze oxen that breathed fire before he could take a certain treasure. A potion from this man’s future wife protected him from the oxen’s fiery breath before he sowed a dragon’s teeth like seeds.
tossups.r: Those teeth grew into warriors that this man defeated by throwing a single stone among them. For 10 points, name this leader of the Argonauts who sought the Golden Fleece with help from Medea.

tossups.p: This man’s crew once camped on the all-female island of Lemnos, where he fathered twins with its queen before his companions urged him to continue the voyage. Later, this man’s ship squeezed through the Symplegades, narrowly avoiding being crushed between two moving rocks.
tossups.r: This man then faced trials set by King Aeetes to win the Golden Fleece, with help from the king’s daughter, Medea. For 10 points, name this captain of the Argo who led the Argonauts.

tossups.p: This man’s uncle, Pelias, had promised to give up the throne of Iolcus if this man could bring back a certain golden-wooled treasure from the far-off kingdom of Colchis. Along the way, this man’s crew lost the strongman Heracles, who stayed behind searching for a lost companion.
tossups.r: At Colchis, this man won the help of the sorceress Medea to complete his quest. For 10 points, name this hero who led the Argonauts in their search for the Golden Fleece.

tossups.p: On the way home, this man’s ship slipped past the monster Scylla and a deadly whirlpool with help from the sea nymph Thetis. Earlier, this man had agreed to let his new wife murder her own brother, Apsyrtus, during their escape from Colchis.
tossups.r: That marriage ended badly years later in Corinth. For 10 points, name this Greek hero and captain of the Argo who led the Argonauts on the quest for the Golden Fleece.

tossups.p: This man wore only one sandal when he first arrived at his uncle’s court, fulfilling a prophecy that unsettled King Pelias. Before that, this man had been trained in secret by the wise centaur Chiron, far from Iolcus.
tossups.r: Pelias then sent this man to distant Colchis to fetch the Golden Fleece, never expecting him to survive. For 10 points, name this hero who led the Argonauts and later married the sorceress Medea.

trap.title: Jason, or just an Argonaut?
trap.body: Clues about the crew—Heracles, Orpheus, Atalanta, the Sirens, Lemnos—describe the whole expedition, not Jason personally, so “Argonauts” or a crewmate’s name is a tempting but wrong early buzz. “Argo” is the ship, not its captain, and “Golden Fleece” is the prize he sought, not the hero himself.
trap.fix: Listen for what the pronoun is doing: a clue about leading, marrying Medea, or being sent by Pelias points to Jason specifically. A clue naming only another Argonaut’s deed (Heracles’s strength, Orpheus’s music) is not enough on its own to buzz “Jason.”

topics.name: Ra
topics.kicker: Egyptian sun god · Sails the sky by day, battles Apophis by night
topics.dates: Worshipped in Egypt from the Old Kingdom (c. 2600 BCE)
topics.briefing: Ancient Egyptians believed the sun crossing the sky was really a god sailing a glowing boat called the solar barge. Every single night, that god sailed on through the underworld, where a giant serpent named Apophis tried to swallow him and stop the sunrise forever. He won every night for thousands of years in a row, which is exactly why the Egyptians trusted the sun to always rise again.

trap.title: Which Egyptian sun god?
trap.body: Ra shares the sun with several other Egyptian gods: Horus is a separate falcon god until he merges with Ra as Ra-Horakhty, Amun is a separate Theban god until he merges with Ra as Amun-Ra, and Aten is a more abstract sun-disk deity that the pharaoh Akhenaten promoted above all others, including Ra, for a short time. A clue naming only Horus, Amun, or Aten by themselves points to a different answer line.
trap.fix: If the clue says this god battles Apophis nightly in a solar barge, sails from Heliopolis, or is the grandfather of Geb and Nut, say Ra. If the clue is specifically about Akhenaten’s religious revolution, the answer is Aten, not Ra.
